osces.title: Pulmonary Hypertension - Right Heart Catheterization Interpretation
objectives: Interpret right heart catheterization haemodynamic measurements
Classify pulmonary hypertension according to WHO functional class
Initiate appropriate targeted therapy for pulmonary arterial hypertension
Assess right ventricular function and cardiac output
Explain vasoreactivity testing and treatment implications
Discuss prognosis and referral for advanced therapies
osces.scenario_stem: You are a medical registrar in the respiratory clinic at a tertiary hospital. Ms Jennifer Walsh, a 52-year-old woman, presents with progressive dyspnoea (NYHA Class III) and has recently undergone right heart catheterization for suspected pulmonary hypertension. Her echocardiogram showed severe pulmonary hypertension (estimated RVSP 85 mmHg) with right ventricular dilatation and impaired function (TAPSE 14 mm). She has no history of left heart disease, chronic lung disease, or thromboembolic disease. The right heart catheterization was performed yesterday. Review the catheterization results, classify her pulmonary hypertension, discuss treatment options, and explain prognosis.

patient_demographics.living_situation: Lives with husband in suburban Sydney

presenting_complaint.chief_complaint: Progressive shortness of breath over 18 months, reduced exercise tolerance, occasional chest tightness
presenting_complaint.severity: Unable to climb stairs without stopping, previously very active (played tennis regularly)
presenting_complaint.pattern: Progressive, worse with exertion, some improvement with rest
associated_symptoms: No chest pain, cough, or haemoptysis
presenting_complaint.impact_on_life: Stopped working 3 months ago due to fatigue and breathlessness, unable to play tennis, struggles with household activities

history_of_presenting_complaint.onset: Gradual onset 18 months ago, initially attributed to deconditioning and stress
history_of_presenting_complaint.progression: Progressive worsening despite initial attempts at exercise rehabilitation
history_of_presenting_complaint.precipitating_factors: No clear precipitant, symptoms worse with any physical exertion
history_of_presenting_complaint.relieving_factors: Rest provides partial relief, no response to bronchodilators (tried by GP)
history_of_presenting_complaint.investigations_to_date: Echocardiogram showed RVSP 85 mmHg, right ventricular dilatation, TAPSE 14 mm, normal left ventricular function (EF 60%), no significant valvular disease. CT pulmonary angiogram excluded chronic thromboembolic disease. High-resolution CT chest showed no interstitial lung disease. Spirometry normal (FEV1/FVC 0.82, FEV1 95% predicted). NT-proBNP elevated at 1,850 pg/mL. 6-minute walk distance 280 metres with oxygen desaturation to 89%.
history_of_presenting_complaint.treatments_tried: Salbutamol inhaler (no benefit), low-dose frusemide 20 mg daily (minimal benefit), ceased due to postural hypotension

conditions: Raynaud's phenomenon (15 years, managed conservatively)
Positive anti-centromere antibodies (tested 5 years ago for Raynaud's)
Mild oesophageal dysmotility on barium swallow (limited systemic sclerosis suspected)
No history of appetite suppressant use
No HIV risk factors
No liver disease
hospitalisations: Admission 6 weeks ago for right heart catheterization workup

conditions: Mother: Systemic sclerosis (died age 68 from pulmonary complications)
Father: Hypertension, type 2 diabetes (alive, age 78)
Sister: Raynaud's phenomenon
No family history of congenital heart disease or sudden cardiac death
family_history.genetic_risk: Significant family history of connective tissue disease

occupation.current: On sick leave from primary school teaching
occupation.exposure: No occupational exposures to lung toxins

exercise.baseline: Previously very active - tennis 3x/week, walking daily

social_history.living_environment: Suburban house, no mould or environmental exposures

physical_examination.general_inspection: Well-groomed woman, appears mildly dyspnoeic at rest, comfortable sitting. No cyanosis. No digital clubbing. Positive Raynaud's phenomenon (pale, then cyanotic fingers with cold exposure). Telangiectasia on face and hands.

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 94% on room air at rest (drops to 89% with minimal exertion)

cardiovascular.inspection: JVP elevated to 6 cm above sternal angle at 45 degrees. Prominent V waves visible. Slight peripheral oedema (1+ pitting to mid-calf bilaterally).
cardiovascular.palpation: Apex beat not displaced. Palpable right ventricular heave at left sternal edge. Normal volume radial pulses bilaterally, regular rhythm.
cardiovascular.auscultation: Heart sounds: Normal S1, loud P2 (pulmonary component of second heart sound). Pansystolic murmur grade 2/6 at left lower sternal edge (tricuspid regurgitation), louder on inspiration. No diastolic murmurs.

respiratory.inspection: Normal chest wall movement, no use of accessory muscles. Trachea central. No scars.
respiratory.palpation: Normal expansion bilaterally. No tenderness. Tactile fremitus normal.
respiratory.auscultation: Vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. No wheeze, crackles, or pleural rub. Good air entry to bases.

abdominal.inspection: Soft, no distension. Cholecystectomy scars visible.
abdominal.palpation: Liver edge palpable 2 cm below right costal margin, smooth, non-tender, pulsatile (tricuspid regurgitation). No splenomegaly. No ascites.

physical_examination.neurological: Alert and oriented. Cranial nerves II-XII intact. Normal power, tone, reflexes, and sensation in all limbs. Gait not assessed due to dyspnoea.
physical_examination.skin: Telangiectasia on face and hands. Mild sclerodactyly (thickened skin on fingers). No rashes or ulcers.
physical_examination.other: Sclerodactyly present. Limited mouth opening (microstomia) - 4 cm interincisor distance (normal >5 cm). Dry mucous membranes.

imaging.result: Right ventricle severely dilated with impaired systolic function (TAPSE 14 mm, normal >17 mm). Right atrium moderately dilated. Estimated right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) 85 mmHg based on tricuspid regurgitation jet. Moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Left ventricle normal size and function (LVEF 60%). No left atrial dilatation. No significant valvular disease. No pericardial effusion. IVC dilated (2.4 cm) with <50% inspiratory collapse (elevated right atrial pressure).
imaging.interpretation: Severe pulmonary hypertension with right heart failure

imaging.result: No evidence of acute or chronic pulmonary embolism. No filling defects. Main pulmonary artery diameter 32 mm (dilated, normal <29 mm). Right ventricle dilated relative to left ventricle (RV/LV ratio 1.4). Patent pulmonary arteries. No interstitial lung disease. No emphysema. Small bilateral pleural effusions.
imaging.interpretation: Excludes chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Confirms pulmonary hypertension.

imaging.result: No evidence of interstitial lung disease. No honeycombing, ground-glass opacification, or reticular abnormality. Minimal basal atelectasis. Dilated pulmonary artery. Enlarged right heart chambers. No bronchiectasis. No emphysema.
imaging.interpretation: Excludes parenchymal lung disease as cause of pulmonary hypertension

imaging.result: Enlarged main pulmonary artery segment. Enlarged right heart border. Clear lung fields. No consolidation or pulmonary oedema. Cardiothoracic ratio 0.54 (mildly increased).
imaging.interpretation: Consistent with pulmonary hypertension and right heart enlargement

laboratory.interpretation: Markedly elevated - indicates right ventricular strain and heart failure

laboratory.result: Bilirubin 22 μmol/L (3-20), ALT 28 U/L (5-40), AST 32 U/L (5-40), ALP 88 U/L (30-110), Albumin 38 g/L (35-50). GGT 35 U/L (5-55).
laboratory.interpretation: Mild hyperbilirubinaemia (congestive hepatopathy from right heart failure). Otherwise normal.

laboratory.result: Creatinine 72 μmol/L (45-90), eGFR >90 mL/min/1.73m². Urea 5.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5).
ANA positive 1:640 (centromere pattern). Anti-centromere antibodies strongly positive. Rheumatoid factor negative. Anti-Scl-70 negative. Anti-RNA polymerase III negative.
laboratory.interpretation: Strongly positive anti-centromere antibodies - diagnostic of limited systemic sclerosis (lcSSc). Pattern associated with pulmonary arterial hypertension.

pulmonary_function.result: FEV1 2.85 L (95% predicted), FVC 3.48 L (97% predicted), FEV1/FVC ratio 0.82 (normal >0.70). No significant bronchodilator response.
pulmonary_function.interpretation: Normal spirometry - excludes obstructive or restrictive lung disease

pulmonary_function.result: Total lung capacity (TLC) 4.8 L (92% predicted), Residual volume (RV) 1.3 L (88% predicted). RV/TLC ratio 0.27 (normal <0.35).
pulmonary_function.interpretation: Normal lung volumes - excludes interstitial lung disease
Reduced diffusion capacity - consistent with pulmonary vascular disease

pulmonary_function.result: Distance 280 metres (predicted >500 metres for age/gender). Baseline SpO2 94%, nadir SpO2 89% (>4% desaturation). Borg dyspnoea score at end: 7/10. Heart rate increase from 88 to 128 bpm.
pulmonary_function.interpretation: Severely reduced exercise capacity with significant oxygen desaturation. Functional capacity NYHA Class III.

haemodynamics.result: Right atrial pressure (RAP) 12 mmHg (normal 0-5 mmHg). Right ventricular pressure 78/12 mmHg. Pulmonary artery pressure (PAP) 78/32 mmHg, mean PAP 52 mmHg (normal <20 mmHg). Pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) 10 mmHg (normal 6-12 mmHg). Cardiac output (Fick method) 3.8 L/min. Cardiac index 2.2 L/min/m² (normal 2.5-4.0 L/min/m²). Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) 11.1 Wood units (normal <2 Wood units). Systemic vascular resistance 18 Wood units. Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) 58% (normal 65-75%). Vasoreactivity testing with inhaled nitric oxide (20 ppm for 5 minutes): PAP decreased to 68/28 mmHg, mean PAP 46 mmHg (12% reduction, but did not meet positive vasoreactivity criteria of ≥10 mmHg decrease and mean PAP <40 mmHg). Cardiac output increased to 4.2 L/min.
haemodynamics.interpretation: SEVERE PRE-CAPILLARY PULMONARY HYPERTENSION: Mean PAP 52 mmHg (diagnostic threshold >20 mmHg), normal PAWP 10 mmHg (excludes post-capillary/left heart disease), PVR markedly elevated at 11.1 WU (diagnostic threshold >2 WU). Classification: WHO Group 1 Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) associated with connective tissue disease (limited systemic sclerosis). WHO Functional Class III. Negative vasoreactivity test (not candidate for calcium channel blocker monotherapy). Reduced cardiac output and cardiac index indicate right ventricular failure. Elevated RAP and reduced SvO2 indicate poor prognosis markers.

key_findings: Severe pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH): mean PAP 52 mmHg, PVR 11.1 Wood units
Pre-capillary pattern (PAWP normal at 10 mmHg) - excludes left heart disease
WHO Group 1 PAH associated with limited systemic sclerosis (anti-centromere positive)
WHO Functional Class III (severely limited exercise tolerance)
Right heart failure: elevated RAP (12 mmHg), reduced cardiac index (2.2 L/min/m²)
Negative vasoreactivity testing - NOT candidate for calcium channel blocker therapy
Poor prognostic markers: elevated RAP, low cardiac index, reduced SvO2 (58%), 6MWD <300m
Limited systemic sclerosis confirmed: anti-centromere antibodies, Raynaud's, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) associated with connective tissue disease (limited systemic sclerosis) - WHO Group 1
supporting_features: Right heart catheterization: mean PAP 52 mmHg, PVR 11.1 WU, normal PAWP (pre-capillary pattern)
Limited systemic sclerosis: anti-centromere antibodies, Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia
Family history: mother died of systemic sclerosis with pulmonary complications
Excluded other causes: normal spirometry/lung volumes, no CTEPH on CTPA, no left heart disease

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH) - WHO Group 4
against_features: CTPA showed no filling defects or chronic thromboembolic changes
No history of previous venous thromboembolism
V/Q scan would be definitive if doubt remained (not performed as CTPA sufficient)

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Pulmonary Hypertension due to left heart disease - WHO Group 2
against_features: PAWP normal at 10 mmHg (pre-capillary, not post-capillary)
Echocardiogram: normal left ventricular size and function (EF 60%)
No left atrial dilatation, no significant valvular disease
No history of hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, or cardiomyopathy

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Pulmonary Hypertension due to lung disease/hypoxia - WHO Group 3
against_features: Normal spirometry (FEV1/FVC 0.82, no obstruction or restriction)
HRCT chest normal (no interstitial lung disease, no emphysema)
PVR 11.1 WU far exceeds typical Group 3 (usually mild elevation <5 WU)
Oxygen saturation only mildly reduced at rest (94%)

differential_diagnosis.diagnosis: Idiopathic Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (IPAH) - WHO Group 1
against_features: Presence of connective tissue disease (limited systemic sclerosis) makes this secondary PAH
Positive anti-centromere antibodies establish CTD-PAH diagnosis
Classification: PAH associated with connective tissue disease, not idiopathic

clinical_reasoning_points: RIGHT HEART CATHETERIZATION is the gold standard for diagnosing pulmonary hypertension and is MANDATORY for confirming the diagnosis and guiding treatment decisions
Diagnostic criteria for pulmonary hypertension: mean PAP >20 mmHg (updated from previous threshold of ≥25 mmHg in 2018 guidelines)
PRE-CAPILLARY vs POST-CAPILLARY distinction is critical: PAWP ≤15 mmHg indicates pre-capillary (Groups 1, 3, 4, 5), PAWP >15 mmHg indicates post-capillary (Group 2 - left heart disease)
PVR >2 Wood units confirms pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension (in addition to elevated PAP and normal PAWP)

WHO Classification: Group 1 (PAH - includes idiopathic, hereditary, drug-induced, connective tissue disease-associated, congenital heart disease, portal hypertension), Group 2 (left heart disease), Group 3 (lung disease/hypoxia), Group 4 (CTEPH), Group 5 (unclear/multifactorial)

LIMITED SYSTEMIC SCLEROSIS (lcSSc) has HIGHEST prevalence of PAH among connective tissue diseases (10-15% develop PAH). Anti-centromere antibodies are hallmark of lcSSc and associated with higher PAH risk.

VASOREACTIVITY TESTING with inhaled nitric oxide, IV epoprostenol, or IV adenosine identifies patients who may respond to calcium channel blockers (CCBs). Positive test: ≥10 mmHg decrease in mean PAP to absolute value <40 mmHg, with increased or unchanged cardiac output. Only 10-15% of IPAH patients are vasoreactive, even fewer in CTD-PAH.
This patient's vasoreactivity test was NEGATIVE (mean PAP decreased by 6 mmHg to 46 mmHg, did not reach <40 mmHg threshold), so CCB monotherapy is contraindicated. She requires PAH-targeted therapy.

PROGNOSTIC FACTORS in PAH: Poor prognosis indicated by WHO FC III-IV, 6MWD <300m, elevated RAP >8 mmHg, low cardiac index <2.5 L/min/m², elevated NT-proBNP, low SvO2 <65%. This patient has MULTIPLE poor prognostic markers.

Australian PBS criteria for PAH therapies (endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues, soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators) require: 1) Diagnosis confirmed by RHC, 2) WHO Group 1 PAH, 3) WHO FC II-IV, 4) Prescribed by or in consultation with specialist with expertise in PAH

INITIAL COMBINATION THERAPY (two drugs upfront) is now recommended for intermediate-high and high-risk PAH patients (2022 ESC/ERS Guidelines). Regimen: endothelin receptor antagonist + phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (e.g., ambrisentan + tadalafil, or macitentan + tadalafil).
CTD-PAH patients have WORSE prognosis than IPAH, with 3-year survival 50-60% vs 65-70% for IPAH. Aggressive treatment and early referral to advanced therapy centres are critical.

MONITORING: Serial 6MWT, NT-proBNP, echocardiography every 3-6 months. Repeat RHC at 3-6 months to assess treatment response. Goal: achieve low-risk status (WHO FC I-II, 6MWD >440m, NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL, RAP <8 mmHg, cardiac index ≥2.5 L/min/m²).

ADVANCED THERAPIES for refractory PAH: IV/subcutaneous prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol, treprostinil), lung transplantation. Refer to specialist PAH centre if inadequate response to oral dual therapy within 3-6 months.

SUPPORTIVE MEASURES: Diuretics for fluid overload (frusemide, cautiously to avoid reducing cardiac preload excessively), oxygen therapy if SpO2 <90%, warfarin anticoagulation is CONTROVERSIAL in CTD-PAH (benefit less clear than IPAH, bleeding risk with oesophageal varices if portal hypertension develops). Exercise training in supervised pulmonary rehabilitation improves functional capacity.
CTD-PAH screening: All systemic sclerosis patients should have ANNUAL echocardiography screening for PAH, starting at diagnosis. Earlier detection improves outcomes.

red_flags.flag: Severe pulmonary arterial hypertension with right heart failure (WHO FC III, elevated RAP, low cardiac index, reduced SvO2)
red_flags.action: Urgent initiation of PAH-specific therapy. Refer to specialist PAH centre. Risk of right heart decompensation and sudden cardiac death.

red_flags.flag: Multiple poor prognostic markers (RAP 12 mmHg, cardiac index 2.2 L/min/m², SvO2 58%, 6MWD 280m, NT-proBNP 1850 pg/mL)
red_flags.action: High-risk patient. Requires aggressive upfront combination therapy (dual oral therapy) and close monitoring. Consider early evaluation for advanced therapies (parenteral prostanoids, lung transplantation).

red_flags.flag: Connective tissue disease-associated PAH (limited systemic sclerosis) - worse prognosis than idiopathic PAH
red_flags.action: CTD-PAH has higher mortality than IPAH. Requires multidisciplinary care (rheumatology, respiratory, cardiology). Monitor for other organ involvement (renal crisis, ILD progression).

red_flags.flag: Negative vasoreactivity test - calcium channel blocker monotherapy contraindicated
red_flags.action: Do NOT use CCBs alone (risk of hypotension and worsening right heart failure in non-vasoreactive patients). Requires PAH-targeted therapy.

learning_outcomes: Interpret right heart catheterization haemodynamic values to diagnose and classify pulmonary hypertension
Differentiate pre-capillary (Groups 1, 3, 4, 5) from post-capillary (Group 2) pulmonary hypertension using PAWP
Recognize WHO Group 1 PAH associated with connective tissue disease (limited systemic sclerosis)
Understand vasoreactivity testing and its role in selecting calcium channel blocker therapy
Identify poor prognostic markers in PAH (elevated RAP, low cardiac index, reduced 6MWD, elevated NT-proBNP)
Initiate appropriate PAH-specific therapy: upfront combination therapy for intermediate-high/high-risk patients
Explain PBS criteria for PAH medications in Australia
Discuss prognosis with patients: CTD-PAH has 3-year survival 50-60%, worse than IPAH
Outline monitoring plan: serial 6MWT, NT-proBNP, echocardiography, repeat RHC to assess treatment response
Recognize indications for referral to advanced PAH centre and lung transplantation evaluation

key_tasks: Review and correctly interpret right heart catheterization results
Classify pulmonary hypertension as WHO Group 1 PAH associated with connective tissue disease
Explain the significance of normal PAWP (pre-capillary pattern) and elevated PVR
Interpret vasoreactivity testing and explain why calcium channel blockers are contraindicated
Identify poor prognostic markers and assign risk stratification (high-risk patient)
Initiate appropriate PAH-specific therapy: recommend upfront combination therapy
Discuss medication options (endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors)
Explain monitoring plan and goals of therapy
Discuss prognosis honestly and sensitively
Arrange referral to specialist PAH centre for ongoing management
candidate_challenges: Interpreting complex haemodynamic data from right heart catheterization
Understanding the distinction between pre-capillary and post-capillary pulmonary hypertension
Recognizing that vasoreactivity testing was negative and CCBs are contraindicated
Knowing current guidelines recommend upfront combination therapy for high-risk patients
Communicating poor prognosis sensitively while maintaining hope and discussing treatment options
Familiarity with Australian PBS criteria for PAH medications
Understanding the association between limited systemic sclerosis and PAH
Identifying all prognostic markers and their implications
pass_criteria: Correctly interprets RHC: mean PAP 52 mmHg, PVR 11.1 WU, normal PAWP 10 mmHg = pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension
Classifies as WHO Group 1 PAH associated with connective tissue disease (limited systemic sclerosis)
Recognizes negative vasoreactivity test and states CCB monotherapy is contraindicated
Identifies at least 3 poor prognostic markers (e.g., WHO FC III, elevated RAP, low CI, reduced 6MWD, elevated NT-proBNP)
Recommends upfront combination therapy with two PAH-specific drugs (e.g., endothelin receptor antagonist + PDE-5 inhibitor)
Discusses need for specialist referral to PAH centre
Explains monitoring plan (serial 6MWT, NT-proBNP, echocardiography, repeat RHC)
Discusses prognosis: CTD-PAH has 3-year survival ~50-60%, emphasizes importance of treatment
Communicates clearly and sensitively with patient, addresses concerns, checks understanding
common_errors: Failing to recognize the significance of normal PAWP (excluding left heart disease)
Misinterpreting vasoreactivity test as positive and recommending calcium channel blockers (dangerous error)
Recommending monotherapy instead of upfront combination therapy for high-risk patient
Not recognizing the association between limited systemic sclerosis and PAH
Failing to identify multiple poor prognostic markers
Not discussing prognosis or providing unrealistic expectations
Not arranging specialist referral to PAH centre
Confusing WHO classification groups (e.g., classifying as Group 3 lung disease)

marking_criteria.criterion: Correctly interprets right heart catheterization haemodynamics
marking_criteria.description: States mean PAP 52 mmHg (severe elevation), PVR 11.1 WU (markedly elevated), normal PAWP 10 mmHg (pre-capillary pattern, excludes left heart disease)
Diagnoses WHO Group 1 Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension associated with connective tissue disease (limited systemic sclerosis, anti-centromere antibody positive)

Recognizes negative vasoreactivity test (mean PAP decreased by 6 mmHg to 46 mmHg, did not meet criteria of ≥10 mmHg decrease to <40 mmHg). States calcium channel blocker monotherapy is contraindicated.

marking_criteria.criterion: Identifies prognostic markers and assigns risk stratification
marking_criteria.description: Identifies ≥3 poor prognostic markers: WHO FC III, 6MWD <300m (280m), elevated RAP (12 mmHg), low cardiac index (2.2 L/min/m²), elevated NT-proBNP (1850 pg/mL), low SvO2 (58%). Classifies as high-risk patient.

Recommends upfront combination therapy with two PAH drugs (endothelin receptor antagonist + phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, e.g., ambrisentan + tadalafil, or macitentan + tadalafil). Explains rationale: high-risk patient requires aggressive treatment.

Discusses at least two PAH drug classes: 1) Endothelin receptor antagonists (ambrisentan, bosentan, macitentan) - block vasoconstriction and remodelling. 2) Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) - promote vasodilation via nitric oxide pathway. Mentions PBS criteria require specialist prescription and RHC-confirmed diagnosis.

marking_criteria.criterion: Outlines monitoring plan and treatment goals
marking_criteria.description: Recommends serial monitoring: 6-minute walk test, NT-proBNP, echocardiography every 3-6 months. Repeat RHC at 3-6 months to assess haemodynamic response. Goals: achieve WHO FC I-II, 6MWD >440m, NT-proBNP <300 pg/mL, RAP <8 mmHg, cardiac index ≥2.5.

Explains CTD-PAH has 3-year survival ~50-60%, worse than idiopathic PAH. Emphasizes importance of treatment to improve outcomes. Balances honesty with hope (treatment can improve symptoms, functional capacity, and prolong life). Addresses patient's concerns and checks understanding.

Refers to specialist pulmonary hypertension centre for ongoing management. Coordinates care with rheumatology (systemic sclerosis management). Discusses potential need for advanced therapies (parenteral prostanoids, lung transplantation) if inadequate response.

Discusses diuretics for fluid overload (careful dose titration), oxygen therapy for hypoxia (SpO2 <90%), supervised exercise training, pneumococcal and influenza vaccination. Mentions pregnancy contraindication (high maternal mortality risk).

Uses clear, jargon-free language. Checks patient understanding. Addresses emotional impact of diagnosis. Involves patient in treatment decisions. Provides written information and support resources (Pulmonary Hypertension Association of Australia).
Professional demeanour. Structured approach to reviewing results and discussing management. Efficient use of time (15 minutes). Summarizes key points at end.

guidelines: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension (2022)
Pulmonary Hypertension Society of Australia and New Zealand (PHSANZ) Consensus Statement
Australian Rheumatology Association Systemic Sclerosis Management Guidelines
PBS criteria for PAH medications (endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors, prostacyclin analogues)
medications: Ambrisentan (endothelin receptor antagonist) - PBS authority required, specialist prescription
Macitentan (endothelin receptor antagonist) - PBS authority required
Tadalafil (PDE-5 inhibitor) - PBS listed for PAH
Sildenafil (PDE-5 inhibitor) - PBS listed for PAH
Riociguat (soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator) - PBS authority for CTEPH or PAH
Selexipag (prostacyclin receptor agonist) - PBS authority for PAH inadequately controlled on dual oral therapy
Epoprostenol (IV prostacyclin) - hospital use, specialist PAH centres
Warfarin - controversial in CTD-PAH, consider in IPAH
Frusemide - PBS listed, for fluid overload

Australian Lung Transplant Programs: St Vincent's Hospital Sydney, The Alfred Hospital Melbourne
Pulmonary Hypertension Association of Australia - patient support and education

osces.title: Cystic Fibrosis - Multidisciplinary Management and CFTR Modulators
objectives: Assess acute exacerbation of cystic fibrosis and prescribe appropriate antibiotics
Optimize airway clearance, nutritional support, and pancreatic enzyme replacement
Discuss eligibility for CFTR modulator therapy and expected benefits
Coordinate multidisciplinary care (respiratory, dietetics, physiotherapy, psychology)
Address complications: diabetes, liver disease, reduced fertility
Discuss lung transplantation referral criteria and timing

clinical_context.setting: Adult cystic fibrosis clinic, tertiary hospital

osces.scenario_stem: You are a respiratory medicine registrar in the adult cystic fibrosis (CF) clinic at a tertiary hospital. Mr Daniel Kim, a 28-year-old man with cystic fibrosis (homozygous F508del mutation), presents with an acute pulmonary exacerbation. He reports increased cough, sputum production (green, purulent), fatigue, and weight loss (3 kg over 2 weeks). His FEV1 today is 38% predicted (baseline 48% predicted). He has chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization and CF-related diabetes. He is interested in CFTR modulator therapy (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor), which has recently become PBS-listed for F508del homozygous patients. Assess the exacerbation, initiate treatment, discuss CFTR modulator eligibility, and coordinate multidisciplinary care.

history_of_presenting_complaint.onset: Gradual onset 2 weeks ago, initially thought it was a 'cold'
history_of_presenting_complaint.progression: Progressive worsening despite adherence to usual CF medications and airway clearance
history_of_presenting_complaint.precipitating_factors: No clear trigger, girlfriend had viral URTI 3 weeks ago (possible precipitant)

history_of_presenting_complaint.treatments_tried: Increased physiotherapy frequency, nebulized salbutamol and hypertonic saline, completed all medications. No improvement.

imaging.result: Hyperinflation with flattened hemidiaphragms. Increased bronchovascular markings throughout both lung fields (bronchiectasis). New right upper lobe consolidation (patchy opacity). Prominent pulmonary arteries. Cystic changes and bronchiectasis most marked in upper lobes bilaterally. No pneumothorax. No pleural effusion. Heart size normal.
imaging.interpretation: Acute right upper lobe consolidation superimposed on chronic CF lung changes (bronchiectasis, hyperinflation). Consistent with acute pulmonary exacerbation.

Cystic changes and bullae in apices. Ground-glass opacities in upper lobes (tree-in-bud pattern - bronchiolar inflammation). Mosaic attenuation (air trapping). No evidence of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. No mycetoma. Minimal bronchiectasis in lower lobes.
imaging.interpretation: Advanced CF lung disease with upper lobe predominant bronchiectasis. Modified Bhalla score 14/25 (moderate-severe CF lung disease).

Sensitive to piperacillin/tazobactam, tobramycin, meropenem, ceftazidime, colistin. No methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) isolated in past 2 years. Aspergillus fumigatus isolated once (18 months ago, treated for ABPA, resolved).
microbiology.interpretation: Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization with developing antibiotic resistance (fluoroquinolone-resistant). Requires IV combination antibiotics for exacerbations (two anti-pseudomonal agents for synergy).

other.result: Homozygous F508del mutation (c.1521_1523delCTT; p.Phe508del on both CFTR alleles)
other.interpretation: Most common CF mutation worldwide (~70% of CF alleles). Homozygous F508del patients are ELIGIBLE for elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta) CFTR modulator therapy (PBS-listed in Australia since 2020 for age ≥6 years with at least one F508del mutation).

other.result: Lumbar spine T-score -1.8 (osteopenia). Femoral neck T-score -1.4 (osteopenia).
other.interpretation: Osteopenia (T-score between -1.0 and -2.5). Risk factors: malabsorption, vitamin D deficiency, chronic corticosteroid use (not current), hypogonadism, chronic disease. Requires calcium, vitamin D supplementation, weight-bearing exercise.

clinical_reasoning_points: CYSTIC FIBROSIS is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the CFTR gene (chromosome 7), encoding the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator protein (chloride channel). Defective CFTR leads to thick, viscous secretions in lungs, pancreas, liver, intestines, and reproductive tract.

F508DEL MUTATION is the most common CF mutation (present in ~70% of CF alleles worldwide). It causes misfolding and degradation of CFTR protein, preventing it from reaching the cell membrane. Homozygous F508del patients have SEVERE disease phenotype.

ACUTE PULMONARY EXACERBATION is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in CF. Defined by Fuchs criteria (≥4 of 12 symptoms/signs): increased cough, sputum production/change, dyspnoea, malaise/fatigue, fever, anorexia/weight loss, sinus pain/tenderness, change in sinus discharge, physical exam findings (crackles/wheeze), FEV1 decline ≥10%, CXR changes, leukocytosis.

PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA is the dominant pathogen in adult CF (chronic colonization in 60-80% of adults). Develops mucoid phenotype (biofilm production), difficult to eradicate. Chronic infection associated with accelerated lung function decline, increased exacerbations, higher mortality.

IV ANTIBIOTIC TREATMENT for CF exacerbations requires TWO anti-pseudomonal agents (synergistic effect, prevent resistance). Common combinations: piperacillin/tazobactam + tobramycin, ceftazidime + tobramycin, meropenem + tobramycin. Duration: 14 days (minimum, may extend to 21 days if slow response). Dose based on previous sensitivities.

CFTR MODULATOR THERAPY represents a paradigm shift in CF treatment - addresses the UNDERLYING DEFECT (corrects CFTR protein function) rather than treating symptoms. Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta): Triple combination highly effective for F508del homozygous and heterozygous patients.

PBS CRITERIA for elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta) in Australia: Age ≥6 years, confirmed CF diagnosis, CFTR genotype with at least one F508del mutation (homozygous or heterozygous), FEV1 <90% predicted OR pancreatic insufficiency. Authority prescription required, must be prescribed by CF specialist. Cost: ~$250,000/year (PBS-subsidized, patient pays standard PBS co-payment).

EXPECTED BENEFITS of CFTR modulators in F508del homozygous patients: Absolute FEV1 improvement 10-14 percentage points, reduced pulmonary exacerbations (50-60% reduction), weight gain (2-4 kg), improved quality of life, sweat chloride normalization, potential to delay/prevent need for lung transplantation. Onset: within 4-12 weeks.

MULTIDISCIPLINARY CF CARE is essential: Respiratory physician (coordination), CF nurse specialist (education, adherence), physiotherapist (airway clearance techniques), dietitian (high-calorie diet, pancreatic enzyme optimization), psychologist (mental health support), endocrinologist (CFRD management), social worker (disability support, employment).

AIRWAY CLEARANCE is a cornerstone of CF management. Techniques: Positive expiratory pressure (PEP) devices, high-frequency chest wall oscillation (The Vest), autogenic drainage, Active Cycle of Breathing Technique (ACBT). Recommended: ≥2 sessions/day when well, increased frequency during exacerbations (3-4 sessions/day).

NUTRITIONAL MANAGEMENT: CF patients require 120-150% of normal caloric intake (increased energy expenditure from increased work of breathing, chronic infection). Target BMI >22 kg/m² for adults (associated with better lung function, survival). Pancreatic enzyme replacement essential (90% of CF patients have pancreatic insufficiency). Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) supplementation required.

CF-RELATED DIABETES (CFRD) prevalence: 20% by age 20, 50% by age 30. Pathophysiology: Pancreatic fibrosis and fatty infiltration → insulin deficiency (NOT insulin resistance like Type 2 DM). Management: Insulin therapy (basal-bolus regimen), carbohydrate counting. HbA1c target <7% (<53 mmol/mol). Annual OGTT screening from age 10.

CF-RELATED LIVER DISEASE: Spectrum from hepatic steatosis to biliary cirrhosis with portal hypertension. Prevalence: 20-30% of CF adults. Monitoring: Annual LFTs, ultrasound every 1-2 years, endoscopy for varices if cirrhosis/portal hypertension. Treatment: Ursodeoxycholic acid (improves bile flow), manage portal hypertension complications.

LUNG TRANSPLANTATION REFERRAL CRITERIA: FEV1 <30% predicted, rapid lung function decline despite optimal therapy, increasing frequency/severity of exacerbations requiring ICU, refractory pneumothorax, massive haemoptysis. Timing: Refer when FEV1 approaching 30% (median wait time 6-12 months in Australia). Post-transplant 5-year survival ~60%.

CONTRACEPTION AND FERTILITY COUNSELLING: Males with CF are 98% infertile due to congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD). Sperm production normal, can father children via assisted reproductive technology (testicular sperm extraction + IVF/ICSI). Females have reduced fertility (thick cervical mucus), but many conceive naturally. Pregnancy in CF requires multidisciplinary care (high-risk obstetrics, CF team), best outcomes if FEV1 >50% and good nutrition pre-conception.

red_flags.flag: FEV1 baseline 48% predicted (severe lung disease, approaching transplant referral threshold of <30%)
red_flags.action: Discuss lung transplantation candidacy and timing with patient. Refer to transplant centre for evaluation if FEV1 continues to decline despite CFTR modulators and optimal management.

red_flags.flag: Chronic hypoxic respiratory failure (baseline SpO2 93-94% on 2 L/min O2, nocturnal desaturations)
red_flags.action: Continue long-term oxygen therapy. Ensure adequate oxygen prescription (2 L/min continuous, increased to 4 L/min during exacerbation). Monitor for CO2 retention (consider ABG if drowsy, confusion develops).

red_flags.flag: Significant weight loss (3 kg in 2 weeks, BMI 19.7 kg/m²) and hypoalbuminaemia (32 g/L)
red_flags.action: Urgent dietitian review. Optimize nutrition: high-calorie oral supplements, consider nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding if unable to maintain weight with oral intake. Optimize pancreatic enzyme replacement (increase dose if steatorrhea). IV nutrition during exacerbation if inadequate oral intake.

red_flags.flag: Suboptimal diabetes control (HbA1c 7.8%, target <7%) during exacerbation
red_flags.action: Acute illness and infection worsen hyperglycaemia. Increase insulin doses during exacerbation. Frequent blood glucose monitoring (4-6 times/day). Endocrinology/diabetes educator input. Optimize control before starting CFTR modulators (can affect glucose metabolism).

red_flags.flag: Fluoroquinolone-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (previous cultures resistant to ciprofloxacin)
red_flags.action: Use IV combination therapy (piperacillin/tazobactam + tobramycin) based on previous sensitivities. Avoid oral fluoroquinolones (ineffective). Monitor tobramycin levels (nephrotoxic, ototoxic). Tailor antibiotics when final sensitivities available.

red_flags.flag: CF-related liver disease with hepatomegaly and hypoalbuminaemia (potential portal hypertension)
red_flags.action: Continue ursodeoxycholic acid. Monitor for varices (last endoscopy 12 months ago, repeat if clinical deterioration). Avoid hepatotoxic drugs. Monitor INR, albumin (synthetic function). Refer hepatology if liver function worsens.

red_flags.flag: Depression and anxiety (seeing psychologist, challenging diagnosis and prognosis)
red_flags.action: Continue psychology support. Screen for depression/anxiety at each visit (PHQ-9, GAD-7 questionnaires). Discuss CFTR modulators' potential to improve quality of life and prognosis (may alleviate psychological burden). Consider antidepressant medication if symptoms severe.

pass_criteria: Diagnoses acute CF pulmonary exacerbation, cites key features (increased symptoms, FEV1 decline, fever, CRP elevation, new CXR infiltrate)
Prescribes appropriate IV antibiotics: two anti-pseudomonal agents (e.g., piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV 8-hourly + tobramycin 10 mg/kg IV daily, levels-based dosing). Duration 14 days minimum.
Identifies patient as eligible for CFTR modulator therapy (homozygous F508del, FEV1 <90%, pancreatic insufficiency)
Explains elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor benefits: FEV1 improvement ~10-14%, reduced exacerbations ~50%, weight gain, QOL improvement
Discusses multidisciplinary management: physiotherapy (airway clearance), dietitian (nutrition, weight gain), endocrinology (CFRD optimization)
Addresses nutritional concerns (BMI 19.7, weight loss 3 kg, target BMI >22, high-calorie diet, optimize pancreatic enzymes)
Recognizes need for airway clearance intensification during exacerbation (3-4 sessions/day)
Discusses prognosis sensitively: FEV1 48% indicates severe disease, CFTR modulators may stabilize/improve lung function, potential to delay transplant
Addresses psychosocial support (psychology, depression/anxiety management, work adjustments, peer support groups)
common_errors: Prescribing single IV antibiotic instead of combination therapy (fails to provide synergy, allows resistance development)
Choosing oral antibiotics for severe exacerbation (inadequate for Pseudomonas aeruginosa in CF)
Not recognizing CFTR modulator eligibility (missing opportunity for disease-modifying therapy)
Overestimating or underestimating CFTR modulator benefits (realistic expectations: significant but not curative)
Failing to address multiple comorbidities (CFRD, liver disease, nutrition, bone health)
Not discussing lung transplantation (relevant for FEV1 <50%, patient should be aware of criteria)
Inadequate psychosocial assessment (missing depression, work challenges, relationship concerns)
Not coordinating multidisciplinary care (CF management requires team approach)

marking_criteria.criterion: Assesses acute pulmonary exacerbation severity and prescribes appropriate IV antibiotic therapy
marking_criteria.description: Diagnoses acute CF exacerbation (Fuchs criteria ≥4 features met). Prescribes combination IV antibiotics: piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV 8-hourly + tobramycin 10 mg/kg IV daily (levels-based dosing). Duration 14 days minimum. Explains rationale: synergy, prevent resistance, target Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Mentions monitoring: tobramycin levels (peak/trough), renal function, audiology.

marking_criteria.criterion: Identifies CFTR modulator eligibility and discusses therapy
marking_criteria.description: Recognizes patient meets PBS criteria: homozygous F508del, FEV1 38% (<90%), pancreatic insufficiency, age ≥6 years. Recommends elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (Trikafta). Explains mechanism: corrector + potentiator drugs improve CFTR protein function at cell membrane. Discusses initiation: requires specialist prescription, baseline LFTs, ophthalmology review (cataracts risk in children, not adults).

marking_criteria.criterion: Explains expected benefits and timeline of CFTR modulators
marking_criteria.description: Discusses realistic benefits: Absolute FEV1 increase 10-14 percentage points (patient's FEV1 may improve from 48% to 58-62%), 50-60% reduction in exacerbations, weight gain 2-4 kg, improved quality of life, sweat chloride normalization. Timeline: benefits within 4-12 weeks. Long-term: may stabilize disease, delay/prevent lung transplantation.

Addresses weight loss (3 kg in 2 weeks, BMI 19.7 kg/m²). Refers to CF dietitian urgently. Recommends: high-calorie oral supplements, optimize pancreatic enzyme dose (may need to increase), target caloric intake 3,000-3,500 kcal/day. Target BMI >22 kg/m². Discusses potential for NG/PEG feeding if oral intake insufficient. Mentions CFTR modulators often improve appetite and weight gain.

Recognizes suboptimal control (HbA1c 7.8%, target <7%). Recommends: increase insulin doses during exacerbation (acute illness increases insulin resistance), frequent blood glucose monitoring (4-6x/day), carbohydrate counting review with diabetes educator. Optimize control before starting CFTR modulators. Long-term: dietitian input for weight gain without worsening diabetes.

marking_criteria.criterion: Intensifies airway clearance and respiratory support
marking_criteria.description: Recommends increased airway clearance frequency: 3-4 sessions/day during exacerbation (from usual 2/day). Continues nebulized hypertonic saline 7%, nebulized salbutamol before physiotherapy. Refers to physiotherapist for technique optimization. Continues oxygen therapy (currently 4 L/min, aim SpO2 ≥92%). Monitors for CO2 retention (consider ABG if clinical concern).

Plans multidisciplinary input: CF nurse specialist (adherence, education), physiotherapist (airway clearance), dietitian (nutrition optimization), endocrinology/diabetes educator (CFRD), psychologist (depression, anxiety, coping), social worker (disability support, employment). Schedules follow-up in CF clinic (2-4 weeks post-IV antibiotics to reassess FEV1 response).

Discusses prognosis honestly: FEV1 48% indicates severe lung disease, median survival for CF patients with FEV1 <30% is 2-3 years without transplant. CFTR modulators transformative: may stabilize lung function, reduce decline, delay/prevent transplantation. Mentions lung transplant as option if FEV1 continues to decline to <30% or refractory exacerbations. Balances realism with hope.

Explores impact on work, relationships, mental health. Validates concerns about future. Discusses depression/anxiety management (continue psychology, consider medication if needed). Fertility counselling: CBAVD (infertile), sperm retrieval + IVF option if desires children. Encourages peer support (CF Foundation, online CF communities, with infection control precautions). Discusses employment rights (disability discrimination protections).

Uses clear, jargon-free language when explaining CFTR modulators and management plan. Checks understanding frequently. Empathetic and supportive tone when discussing prognosis and challenges. Involves patient in treatment decisions (shared decision-making). Provides written information (CFTR modulator fact sheets, CF Foundation resources). Offers contact details for CF nurse specialist for questions.

Professional demeanour. Structured approach: assesses exacerbation → immediate treatment (IV antibiotics) → discusses CFTR modulators → addresses comorbidities → psychosocial support. Efficient use of 15 minutes. Summarizes management plan clearly at end.
